Accountrix AI CFO Training Curriculum - Months 9-12 (Complete)

Month 9: Audit Preparation, Insurance Audits, and Risk Management

Week 1: Financial Audit Preparation and CPA Engagement

Learning Objectives:

  • Master comprehensive year-end audit preparation procedures for construction companies
  • Understand auditor requirements, testing methodologies, and industry-specific risks
  • Learn to prepare detailed audit work papers and supporting schedules
  • Develop expertise in managing the audit process from planning through completion

Comprehensive Lesson Content:

Financial audits in construction are significantly more complex than in other industries due to the project-based nature of operations, percentage-of-completion accounting, and unique risk factors. As CFO, your preparation and management of the audit process directly impacts the cost, duration, and outcome of the engagement.

Understanding Construction Audit Complexity:

Construction companies face unique audit challenges that require specialized preparation:

  1. Revenue Recognition Complexity: ASC 606 percentage-of-completion calculations require extensive documentation and testing
  2. Work-in-Progress Validation: Auditors must verify the accuracy of WIP schedules and underlying cost accumulation
  3. Contract Compliance: Performance obligations, change orders, and claims require detailed review
  4. Multi-Location Operations: Job sites across different states create logistical and documentation challenges
  5. Related Party Transactions: Joint ventures and partnership arrangements need careful examination

Pre-Audit Strategic Planning (90 Days Out):

Audit Firm Selection Criteria:

When selecting or evaluating your audit firm, consider these construction-specific factors:

  • Industry Experience: Minimum 25% of firm's revenue from construction clients
  • Technical Expertise: Demonstrated knowledge of ASC 606, job costing, and WIP accounting
  • Geographic Coverage: Ability to visit multiple job sites efficiently
  • Timing Flexibility: Understanding of construction's seasonal nature and project deadlines
  • Technology Integration: Compatibility with Ledgerline Intacct, JCS Construction, and other systems

Engagement Letter Review:

Your engagement letter should specifically address:

  • Scope of interim and year-end procedures
  • Responsibility for internal control testing
  • Timeline for management representation letters
  • Access requirements for job sites and project documentation
  • Additional services (tax preparation, consulting, etc.)

Audit Planning Meeting Agenda:

Schedule a comprehensive planning meeting 60 days before year-end:

Business Update (30 minutes):

  • New markets entered
  • Major contract awards/completions
  • Organizational changes
  • Technology implementations

Accounting Changes (20 minutes):

  • New accounting standards adopted
  • Changes in estimates or policies
  • System upgrades or conversions

Risk Assessment (45 minutes):

  • Project losses or disputes
  • Customer concentration changes
  • Regulatory compliance issues
  • Internal control deficiencies

Logistics Planning (15 minutes):

  • Document preparation timeline
  • Personnel availability
  • Office space and equipment needs

Comprehensive PBC (Prepared by Client) List:

Core Financial Documents:

Trial Balance Package:

  • Final trial balance in Excel format
  • Monthly trial balances for the year
  • Chart of accounts with descriptions
  • General ledger detail for all accounts

Financial Statements:

  • Draft year-end financial statements
  • Prior year audited statements
  • Monthly financial packages
  • Budget vs. actual comparisons

Supporting Schedules:

  • Bank reconciliations (12 months)
  • Accounts receivable aging
  • Accounts payable aging
  • Inventory rollforwards
  • Fixed asset additions/disposals
  • Debt schedules and loan agreements

Construction-Specific Documentation:

Work-in-Progress Analysis:

  • Detailed WIP schedules by project
  • Percentage completion calculations
  • Cost-to-cost method support
  • Revenue recognition supporting documentation
  • Change order summaries and approvals

Contract Documentation:

  • Original contracts and amendments
  • Change order logs and approvals
  • Claims and dispute documentation
  • Customer correspondence files
  • Legal correspondence regarding contracts

Job Cost Reports:

  • Monthly job cost summaries
  • Labor distribution reports
  • Material usage reports
  • Equipment allocation schedules
  • Subcontractor cost analysis

Internal Control Documentation:

Narrative Descriptions:

Prepare detailed narratives for each major process:

Revenue Recognition Process: "Monthly, project managers submit progress reports including percentage completion estimates based on costs incurred and remaining work to be performed. These reports are reviewed by the operations manager for reasonableness and accuracy. The controller then calculates revenue recognition using the cost-to-cost method, comparing costs incurred to total estimated costs. All calculations are reviewed by the CFO before journal entries are recorded."

Job Costing Process: "Daily timesheets are submitted by field personnel and approved by project superintendents. Payroll costs are allocated to projects based on approved timesheets. Material costs are allocated based on delivery tickets and material transfer documents. Subcontractor costs are recorded when invoices are received and matched to approved subcontracts. Equipment costs are allocated based on daily usage reports."

Process Flow Charts:

Create visual representations of key processes showing:

  • Document flow
  • Approval points
  • System interfaces
  • Control activities
  • Exception handling

Management Representation Letter Preparation:

Begin drafting your management representation letter early, addressing construction-specific items:

Standard Construction Representations:

  • All contracts and change orders are properly recorded and disclosed
  • Revenue recognition follows ASC 606 requirements consistently
  • Percentage completion estimates are based on reasonable methodologies
  • All known or probable losses on contracts have been accrued
  • Claims and disputes have been properly evaluated and recorded
  • All lien waivers and releases have been properly obtained

Subsequent Events Evaluation:

Establish procedures for identifying subsequent events:

  • Major contract awards or cancellations
  • Significant change orders
  • Customer payment delays or disputes
  • Regulatory actions or investigations
  • Natural disasters affecting projects
  • Key personnel departures

Year-End Cutoff Procedures:

Revenue Cutoff Testing:

Document your year-end cutoff procedures:

  • Review the last 10 progress billings before year-end
  • Review the first 10 progress billings after year-end
  • Verify work was performed in the correct period
  • Ensure percentage completion reflects year-end status

Cost Cutoff Testing:

  • Review vendor invoices received in January for December work
  • Verify accruals for uninvoiced costs at year-end
  • Confirm payroll cutoff matches work performed
  • Review material deliveries around year-end

Cost Estimation Process:

Document your process for estimated costs to complete:

  • Monthly Reviews: Project managers update estimates monthly
  • Quarterly Deep Dives: Detailed review with operations team
  • Year-End Validation: Independent review by senior management
  • Documentation: Written support for all significant changes

Week 2: Insurance Audits and Workers' Compensation Management

Learning Objectives:

  • Master the workers' compensation audit process and premium calculations
  • Understand general liability and other insurance audits
  • Learn advanced strategies for managing insurance costs and compliance
  • Develop expertise in certificate of insurance management and tracking

Comprehensive Lesson Content:

Insurance audits in construction can result in significant premium adjustments - often hundreds of thousands of dollars. As CFO, your understanding of the audit process and proactive management can save substantial costs while ensuring proper coverage.

Workers' Compensation Audit Deep Dive:

Understanding Premium Calculations:

Workers' compensation premiums are calculated using this formula: Premium = (Payroll ÷ $100) × Classification Rate × Experience Modification Factor × Schedule Credits/Debits

Detailed Example:

Sunrise Construction has the following annual payroll:

  • Carpenters (Class 5403): $1,200,000 at $8.50 per $100
  • Concrete Workers (Class 5213): $800,000 at $12.75 per $100
  • Office Staff (Class 8810): $300,000 at $0.35 per $100
  • Officers (Class 5606): $400,000 at $3.25 per $100

Base Premium Calculation:

  • Carpenters: ($1,200,000 ÷ 100) × $8.50 = $102,000
  • Concrete: ($800,000 ÷ 100) × $12.75 = $102,000
  • Office: ($300,000 ÷ 100) × $0.35 = $1,050
  • Officers: ($400,000 ÷ 100) × $3.25 = $13,000

Base Premium Total: $218,050

Experience Modification Factor:

If the company's experience mod is 0.92 (8% better than average): Modified Premium: $218,050 × 0.92 = $200,606

Audit Preparation Strategy:

90 Days Before Audit:

  • Document Review: Gather all required records
  • Classification Analysis: Review employee job duties
  • Subcontractor Verification: Confirm certificate validity
  • Payroll Reconciliation: Match to tax returns

Required Documentation:

  • Federal 941 quarterly returns
  • State unemployment reports (SUTA)
  • General ledger payroll entries
  • Individual employee earnings records
  • 1099s issued to subcontractors
  • Certificates of insurance from all subs
  • Cash disbursements journal
  • Payroll registers showing job classifications

Advanced Audit Defense Strategies:

Executive Officer Exemptions:

Many states allow officers to exclude themselves from coverage:

  • Must be true officers (not just titled employees)
  • Must own minimum percentage of company
  • Must file proper exclusion forms
  • Can significantly reduce premiums for owner-operated companies

Example Impact: Owner draws $200,000 salary at 5606 rate of $4.50 per $100:

  • With coverage: $200,000 ÷ 100 × $4.50 = $9,000
  • With exclusion: $0 premium
  • Annual Savings: $9,000

Subcontractor Management:

Certificate Requirements:

Every subcontractor must provide:

  • General Liability: Minimum $1,000,000 per occurrence
  • Workers' Compensation: Statutory limits
  • Additional Insured: Your company named
  • Waiver of Subrogation: Prevents insurance company lawsuits
  • Primary and Non-Contributory: Your policy is excess

Audit Adjustment Categories:

Payroll Adjustments:

  • Underreported Payroll: Additional premium due
  • Misclassified Employees: Rate differential applied
  • Missing Overtime Premium: 1.5x base pay rate
  • Unreported Benefits: Vacation, bonuses included

Subcontractor Adjustments:

  • Missing Certificates: Full premium charged on payments
  • Expired Coverage: Pro-rata premium for uncovered periods
  • Inadequate Limits: Potential policy violations

Example Major Adjustment:

Contractor paid $2,500,000 to subcontractors during audit period:

  • Certificates on file: $1,800,000 (no additional premium)
  • Missing certificates: $700,000
  • Average rate: $8.75 per $100
  • Additional Premium: $700,000 ÷ 100 × $8.75 = $61,250

General Liability Audit Process:

Audit Bases:

GL premiums can be based on:

  • Gross Sales/Receipts: Most common for contractors
  • Payroll: Sometimes used for service companies
  • Area/Square Footage: Rare in construction
  • Units: Homes built, etc.

Sales-Based Calculation Example:

  • Annual gross receipts: $15,000,000
  • Rate: $1.45 per $1,000 of sales
  • Premium: $15,000,000 ÷ 1,000 × $1.45 = $21,750

Audit Defense Strategies:

Exclusions from Sales:

  • Sales tax collected and remitted
  • Finance charges on receivables
  • Returns and allowances
  • Subcontractor costs (in some states)
  • Materials supplied by customer

Experience mods are calculated using a 3-year window, excluding the most recent year:

  • 2024 mod uses 2020, 2021, 2022 experience

  • Updated annually by rating bureaus

Week 3: Internal Controls and Fraud Prevention

Learning Objectives:

  • Design comprehensive internal control systems for construction operations
  • Master fraud prevention and detection techniques specific to construction
  • Understand SOX-level control documentation and testing
  • Learn to implement technology-enabled controls and monitoring

Comprehensive Lesson Content:

Construction companies face unique fraud risks due to high cash flows, remote job sites, valuable materials, and complex subcontractor relationships. As CFO, implementing robust internal controls is essential for protecting assets and ensuring accurate financial reporting.

Construction Fraud Risk Assessment:

High-Risk Areas in Construction:

Payroll Fraud:

  • Ghost employees
  • Inflated hours
  • Unauthorized overtime
  • Misclassified workers

Procurement Fraud:

  • Kickbacks from vendors
  • Bid rigging schemes
  • Inflated invoicing
  • Personal purchases

Cash Manipulation:

  • Customer payment diversion
  • Petty cash theft
  • Check tampering
  • Credit card abuse

Material Theft:

  • Job site pilferage
  • Tool theft
  • Equipment misuse
  • Inventory shrinkage

Revenue Manipulation:

  • Fictitious billings
  • Change order inflation
  • Percentage completion overstatement
  • Related party transactions

Comprehensive Internal Control Framework:

Control Environment:

Strong internal controls start with tone at the top:

Board Oversight:

  • Independent audit committee
  • Regular executive sessions
  • Annual control assessment
  • Ethics policy enforcement

Management Philosophy:

  • Zero tolerance for fraud
  • Mandatory reporting protocols
  • Annual ethics training
  • Background check requirements

Cash Controls - Advanced Framework:

Bank Account Management:

Account Structure:

  • Operating account: Daily operations
  • Payroll account: Zero balance except payroll days
  • Project accounts: Separate for large projects
  • Equipment account: Capital purchases only
  • Tax account: Employment tax deposits

Month 9 Quiz (Enhanced)

Instructions: Choose the best answer for multiple choice questions. Provide complete explanations for short-answer questions. Show all calculations for numerical problems.

  1. Multiple Choice: Under ASC 606, which documentation is MOST critical for auditors reviewing construction revenue recognition?

a) Customer contracts and change orders b) Cash receipt records
c) Percentage completion calculations with supporting cost data d) Progress billing schedules

Answer: c) Percentage completion calculations with supporting cost data

Explanation: While all documentation is important, auditors focus most heavily on the percentage completion calculations because these directly drive revenue recognition. The supporting cost data (actual costs incurred, estimated costs to complete, and total estimated costs) must be detailed and well-supported to validate the revenue recognition calculations under ASC 606.

  1. Multiple Choice: Workers' compensation experience modification factors are calculated using:

a) Current year claims data only b) A 3-year rolling average excluding the most recent year
c) A 5-year average including all years d) Only years with claims activity

Answer: b) A 3-year rolling average excluding the most recent year

Explanation: Experience mods are calculated using a 3-year window that excludes the most recent year to allow for claims to develop. For example, the 2025 mod would use experience from 2021, 2022, and 2023, excluding 2024 to allow sufficient time for claims reporting and settlement.

  1. Short Answer: Explain the three-way match process in construction and why it's critical for fraud prevention.

Answer: The three-way match process compares three documents before authorizing payment: (1) Purchase Order showing what was ordered, (2) Receiving Report confirming what was actually received, and (3) Vendor Invoice requesting payment. This control prevents fraud by ensuring payments are only made for goods/services that were legitimately ordered, actually received, and properly invoiced. Without this control, fictitious invoices could be processed, payments could be made for undelivered goods, or pricing could be manipulated.

  1. Calculation Problem: Calculate the workers' compensation premium for the following annual payroll:

Carpenters: $800,000 at Class 5403, rate $9.25 per $100 Office Staff: $200,000 at Class 8810, rate $0.45 per $100 Experience modification factor: 0.88

Show all work.

Answer:

  • Carpenters: ($800,000 ÷ 100) × $9.25 = $74,000
  • Office Staff: ($200,000 ÷ 100) × $0.45 = $900
  • Base Premium: $74,000 + $900 = $74,900
  • Modified Premium: $74,900 × 0.88 = $65,912
  1. Multiple Choice: Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply to:

a) All construction projects over $10,000 b) Federal construction projects over $2,000 c) State projects over $25,000 d) Commercial projects over $100,000

Answer: b) Federal construction projects over $2,000

Explanation: The Davis-Bacon Act specifically applies to federal construction, alteration, and repair contracts exceeding $2,000. State and local prevailing wage laws are separate requirements with different thresholds.

  1. True/False: Certified payroll reports under Davis-Bacon must be submitted monthly.

Answer: False

Explanation: Certified payroll reports (Form WH-347) must be submitted weekly, not monthly. Each report covers one work week and must be submitted to the contracting agency by the end of the week following the work week covered.

  1. Short Answer: List and explain four red flags that might indicate a ghost employee on the payroll.

Answer:

  1. No tax withholdings: Ghost employees often use fake SSNs that don't generate tax withholdings
  2. Same address as supervisor: May indicate supervisor is creating fictitious employees
  3. Perfect attendance: Never calls in sick, takes vacation, or has any absences (unrealistic)
  4. Round number hours: Always works exactly 40 hours, 80 hours, etc. (lacks natural variation)

Month 9 Test (Enhanced)

Part A: Multiple Choice (20 points - 2 points each)

  1. When preparing for a construction company audit, which schedule requires the MOST detailed supporting documentation?

a) Accounts receivable aging b) Work-in-progress analysis c) Fixed asset rollforward d) Accounts payable listing

Answer: b) Work-in-progress analysis

Explanation: The WIP analysis is the most complex and critical schedule for construction audits, requiring detailed support for costs incurred, estimated costs to complete, percentage completion calculations, and revenue recognition. Auditors spend significant time testing these calculations as they directly impact financial statement accuracy.

  1. Which factor has the GREATEST impact on workers' compensation premium calculations?

a) Number of employees b) Employee classification codes c) Experience modification factor
d) Geographic location

Answer: b) Employee classification codes

Explanation: Classification codes determine the base rates, which can vary dramatically (from $0.35 per $100 for office workers to $25+ per $100 for roofers). While experience mods can adjust premiums by ±50%, classification codes create the foundational rate differential that often exceeds 5,000% between the lowest and highest risk classes.

  1. In a three-way match system, which document should be created FIRST?

a) Purchase order b) Receiving report
c) Vendor invoice d) Payment authorization

Answer: a) Purchase order

Explanation: The purchase order must be created first as it represents the authorized commitment to purchase goods/services. It serves as the control document against which receiving reports and vendor invoices are matched to ensure only authorized purchases are paid.

  1. Under the Davis-Bacon Act, fringe benefits can be satisfied by:

a) Cash payments only b) Bona fide benefit plans only c) Either cash payments or bona fide benefit plans d) Neither - fringe requirements cannot be satisfied

Answer: c) Either cash payments or bona fide benefit plans

Explanation: Davis-Bacon allows contractors flexibility in meeting fringe benefit requirements. They can provide actual benefits (health insurance, pension, etc.) equal to the prevailing rate, pay additional cash wages, or use a combination of both methods.

  1. Which internal control weakness would be classified as a Material Weakness?

a) Missing signatures on purchase orders under $1,000 b) Untimely monthly account reconciliations c) Lack of segregation of duties in cash receipts and disbursements d) Inadequate documentation of policy updates

Answer: c) Lack of segregation of duties in cash receipts and disbursements

Explanation: Material weaknesses create a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement in the financial statements could occur and not be prevented or detected timely. Lack of segregation in cash handling creates significant fraud risk and potential for material errors.

Part B: Short Answer Problems (30 points)

  1. (10 points) Explain the key differences between a financial statement audit, review, and compilation for construction companies. Include the level of assurance provided and typical cost differences.

Answer:

Financial Statement Audit: Provides highest level of assurance through extensive testing of transactions, balances, and internal controls. Auditor expresses an opinion on whether statements are fairly presented in accordance with GAAP. Includes detailed testing of WIP schedules, revenue recognition, and job costs. Typically costs $50,000-$200,000+ depending on company size and complexity.

Review: Provides limited assurance based on analytical procedures and inquiries. No opinion is expressed, only negative assurance ("nothing came to our attention"). Less testing of detailed transactions and internal controls. Typically costs 30-50% less than an audit.

Accountrix AI CFO Training Curriculum - Months 9-12 (Complete)

Month 9: Audit Preparation, Insurance Audits, and Risk Management

Week 1: Financial Audit Preparation and CPA Engagement

Learning Objectives:

  • Master comprehensive year-end audit preparation procedures for construction companies
  • Understand auditor requirements, testing methodologies, and industry-specific risks
  • Learn to prepare detailed audit work papers and supporting schedules
  • Develop expertise in managing the audit process from planning through completion

Comprehensive Lesson Content:

Financial audits in construction are significantly more complex than in other industries due to the project-based nature of operations, percentage-of-completion accounting, and unique risk factors. As CFO, your preparation and management of the audit process directly impacts the cost, duration, and outcome of the engagement.

Understanding Construction Audit Complexity:

Construction companies face unique audit challenges that require specialized preparation:

  1. Revenue Recognition Complexity: ASC 606 percentage-of-completion calculations require extensive documentation and testing
  2. Work-in-Progress Validation: Auditors must verify the accuracy of WIP schedules and underlying cost accumulation
  3. Contract Compliance: Performance obligations, change orders, and claims require detailed review
  4. Multi-Location Operations: Job sites across different states create logistical and documentation challenges
  5. Related Party Transactions: Joint ventures and partnership arrangements need careful examination

Pre-Audit Strategic Planning (90 Days Out):

Audit Firm Selection Criteria:

When selecting or evaluating your audit firm, consider these construction-specific factors:

  • Industry Experience: Minimum 25% of firm's revenue from construction clients
  • Technical Expertise: Demonstrated knowledge of ASC 606, job costing, and WIP accounting
  • Geographic Coverage: Ability to visit multiple job sites efficiently
  • Timing Flexibility: Understanding of construction's seasonal nature and project deadlines
  • Technology Integration: Compatibility with Ledgerline Intacct, JCS Construction, and other systems

Engagement Letter Review:

Your engagement letter should specifically address:

  • Scope of interim and year-end procedures
  • Responsibility for internal control testing
  • Timeline for management representation letters
  • Access requirements for job sites and project documentation
  • Additional services (tax preparation, consulting, etc.)

Audit Planning Meeting Agenda:

Schedule a comprehensive planning meeting 60 days before year-end:

Business Update (30 minutes):

  • New markets entered
  • Major contract awards/completions
  • Organizational changes
  • Technology implementations

Accounting Changes (20 minutes):

  • New accounting standards adopted
  • Changes in estimates or policies
  • System upgrades or conversions

Risk Assessment (45 minutes):

  • Project losses or disputes
  • Customer concentration changes
  • Regulatory compliance issues
  • Internal control deficiencies

Logistics Planning (15 minutes):

  • Document preparation timeline
  • Personnel availability
  • Office space and equipment needs

Comprehensive PBC (Prepared by Client) List:

Core Financial Documents:

Trial Balance Package:

  • Final trial balance in Excel format
  • Monthly trial balances for the year
  • Chart of accounts with descriptions
  • General ledger detail for all accounts

Financial Statements:

  • Draft year-end financial statements
  • Prior year audited statements
  • Monthly financial packages
  • Budget vs. actual comparisons

Supporting Schedules:

  • Bank reconciliations (12 months)
  • Accounts receivable aging
  • Accounts payable aging
  • Inventory rollforwards
  • Fixed asset additions/disposals
  • Debt schedules and loan agreements

Construction-Specific Documentation:

Work-in-Progress Analysis:

  • Detailed WIP schedules by project
  • Percentage completion calculations
  • Cost-to-cost method support

Workers' Compensation Audit Deep Dive:

Understanding Premium Calculations:

Workers' compensation premiums are calculated using this formula: Premium = (Payroll ÷ $100) × Classification Rate × Experience Modification Factor × Schedule Credits/Debits

Detailed Example:

Sunrise Construction has the following annual payroll:

  • Carpenters (Class 5403): $1,200,000 at $8.50 per $100
  • Concrete Workers (Class 5213): $800,000 at $12.75 per $100
  • Office Staff (Class 8810): $300,000 at $0.35 per $100
  • Officers (Class 5606): $400,000 at $3.25 per $100

Base Premium Calculation:

  • Carpenters: ($1,200,000 ÷ 100) × $8.50 = $102,000
  • Concrete: ($800,000 ÷ 100) × $12.75 = $102,000
  • Office: ($300,000 ÷ 100) × $0.35 = $1,050
  • Officers: ($400,000 ÷ 100) × $3.25 = $13,000

Base Premium Total: $218,050

Experience Modification Factor:

If the company's experience mod is 0.92 (8% better than average): Modified Premium: $218,050 × 0.92 = $200,606

Month 9 Quiz (Enhanced)

Instructions: Choose the best answer for multiple choice questions. Provide complete explanations for short-answer questions. Show all calculations for numerical problems.

  1. Multiple Choice: Under ASC 606, which documentation is MOST critical for auditors reviewing construction revenue recognition?

a) Customer contracts and change orders b) Cash receipt records
c) Percentage completion calculations with supporting cost data d) Progress billing schedules

Answer: c) Percentage completion calculations with supporting cost data

Explanation: While all documentation is important, auditors focus most heavily on the percentage completion calculations because these directly drive revenue recognition. The supporting cost data (actual costs incurred, estimated costs to complete, and total estimated costs) must be detailed and well-supported to validate the revenue recognition calculations under ASC 606.

  1. Multiple Choice: Workers' compensation experience modification factors are calculated using:

a) Current year claims data only b) A 3-year rolling average excluding the most recent year
c) A 5-year average including all years d) Only years with claims activity

Answer: b) A 3-year rolling average excluding the most recent year

Explanation: Experience mods are calculated using a 3-year window that excludes the most recent year to allow for claims to develop. For example, the 2025 mod would use experience from 2021, 2022, and 2023, excluding 2024 to allow sufficient time for claims reporting and settlement.

  1. Short Answer: Explain the three-way match process in construction and why it's critical for fraud prevention.

Answer: The three-way match process compares three documents before authorizing payment: (1) Purchase Order showing what was ordered, (2) Receiving Report confirming what was actually received, and (3) Vendor Invoice requesting payment. This control prevents fraud by ensuring payments are only made for goods/services that were legitimately ordered, actually received, and properly invoiced. Without this control, fictitious invoices could be processed, payments could be made for undelivered goods, or pricing could be manipulated.

  1. Calculation Problem: Calculate the workers' compensation premium for the following annual payroll:

Carpenters: $800,000 at Class 5403, rate $9.25 per $100 Office Staff: $200,000 at Class 8810, rate $0.45 per $100 Experience modification factor: 0.88

Show all work.

Answer:

  • Carpenters: ($800,000 ÷ 100) × $9.25 = $74,000
  • Office Staff: ($200,000 ÷ 100) × $0.45 = $900
  • Base Premium: $74,000 + $900 = $74,900
  • Modified Premium: $74,900 × 0.88 = $65,912
  1. Multiple Choice: Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply to:

a) All construction projects over $10,000 b) Federal construction projects over $2,000 c) State projects over $25,000 d) Commercial projects over $100,000

Answer: b) Federal construction projects over $2,000

Explanation: The Davis-Bacon Act specifically applies to federal construction, alteration, and repair contracts exceeding $2,000. State and local prevailing wage laws are separate requirements with different thresholds.

  1. True/False: Certified payroll reports under Davis-Bacon must be submitted monthly.

Answer: False

Explanation: Certified payroll reports (Form WH-347) must be submitted weekly, not monthly. Each report covers one work week and must be submitted to the contracting agency by the end of the week following the work week covered.

  1. Short Answer: List and explain four red flags that might indicate a ghost employee on the payroll.

Answer:

  1. No tax withholdings: Ghost employees often use fake SSNs that don't generate tax withholdings
  2. Same address as supervisor: May indicate supervisor is creating fictitious employees
  3. Perfect attendance: Never calls in sick, takes vacation, or has any absences (unrealistic)
  4. Round number hours: Always works exactly 40 hours, 80 hours, etc. (lacks natural variation)

Month 9 Test (Enhanced)

Part A: Multiple Choice (20 points - 2 points each)

  1. When preparing for a construction company audit, which schedule requires the MOST detailed supporting documentation?

a) Accounts receivable aging b) Work-in-progress analysis c) Fixed asset rollforward d) Accounts payable listing

Answer: b) Work-in-progress analysis

Explanation: The WIP analysis is the most complex and critical schedule for construction audits, requiring detailed support for costs incurred, estimated costs to complete, percentage completion calculations, and revenue recognition. Auditors spend significant time testing these calculations as they directly impact financial statement accuracy.

  1. Which factor has the GREATEST impact on workers' compensation premium calculations?

a) Number of employees b) Employee classification codes c) Experience modification factor
d) Geographic location

Answer: b) Employee classification codes

Explanation: Classification codes determine the base rates, which can vary dramatically (from $0.35 per $100 for office workers to $25+ per $100 for roofers). While experience mods can adjust premiums by ±50%, classification codes create the foundational rate differential that often exceeds 5,000% between the lowest and highest risk classes.

  1. In a three-way match system, which document should be created FIRST?

a) Purchase order b) Receiving report
c) Vendor invoice d) Payment authorization

Answer: a) Purchase order

Explanation: The purchase order must be created first as it represents the authorized commitment to purchase goods/services. It serves as the control document against which receiving reports and vendor invoices are matched to ensure only authorized purchases are paid.

  1. Under the Davis-Bacon Act, fringe benefits can be satisfied by:

a) Cash payments only b) Bona fide benefit plans only c) Either cash payments or bona fide benefit plans d) Neither - fringe requirements cannot be satisfied

Answer: c) Either cash payments or bona fide benefit plans

Explanation: Davis-Bacon allows contractors flexibility in meeting fringe benefit requirements. They can provide actual benefits (health insurance, pension, etc.) equal to the prevailing rate, pay additional cash wages, or use a combination of both methods.

  1. Which internal control weakness would be classified as a Material Weakness?

a) Missing signatures on purchase orders under $1,000 b) Untimely monthly account reconciliations c) Lack of segregation of duties in cash receipts and disbursements d) Inadequate documentation of policy updates

Answer: c) Lack of segregation of duties in cash receipts and disbursements

Explanation: Material weaknesses create a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement in the financial statements could occur and not be prevented or detected timely. Lack of segregation in cash handling creates significant fraud risk and potential for material errors.

Part B: Short Answer Problems (30 points)

  1. (10 points) Explain the key differences between a financial statement audit, review, and compilation for construction companies. Include the level of assurance provided and typical cost differences.

Answer:

Financial Statement Audit: Provides highest level of assurance through extensive testing of transactions, balances, and internal controls. Auditor expresses an opinion on whether statements are fairly presented in accordance with GAAP. Includes detailed testing of WIP schedules, revenue recognition, and job costs. Typically costs $50,000-$200,000+ depending on company size and complexity.

Review: Provides limited assurance based on analytical procedures and inquiries. No opinion is expressed, only negative assurance ("nothing came to our attention"). Less testing of detailed transactions and internal controls. Typically costs 30-50% less than an audit.

Month 9: Audit Preparation, Insurance Audits, and Risk Management

Week 1: Financial Audit Preparation and CPA Engagement

Learning Objectives:

  • Master comprehensive year-end audit preparation procedures for construction companies
  • Understand auditor requirements, testing methodologies, and industry-specific risks
  • Learn to prepare detailed audit work papers and supporting schedules
  • Develop expertise in managing the audit process from planning through completion

Comprehensive Lesson Content:

Financial audits in construction are significantly more complex than in other industries due to the project-based nature of operations, percentage-of-completion accounting, and unique risk factors. As CFO, your preparation and management of the audit process directly impacts the cost, duration, and outcome of the engagement.

Understanding Construction Audit Complexity:

Construction companies face unique audit challenges that require specialized preparation:

  1. Revenue Recognition Complexity: ASC 606 percentage-of-completion calculations require extensive documentation and testing
  2. Work-in-Progress Validation: Auditors must verify the accuracy of WIP schedules and underlying cost accumulation
  3. Contract Compliance: Performance obligations, change orders, and claims require detailed review
  4. Multi-Location Operations: Job sites across different states create logistical and documentation challenges
  5. Related Party Transactions: Joint ventures and partnership arrangements need careful examination

Pre-Audit Strategic Planning (90 Days Out):

Audit Firm Selection Criteria:

When selecting or evaluating your audit firm, consider these construction-specific factors:

  • Industry Experience: Minimum 25% of firm's revenue from construction clients
  • Technical Expertise: Demonstrated knowledge of ASC 606, job costing, and WIP accounting
  • Geographic Coverage: Ability to visit multiple job sites efficiently
  • Timing Flexibility: Understanding of construction's seasonal nature and project deadlines
  • Technology Integration: Compatibility with Ledgerline Intacct, JCS Construction, and other systems

Engagement Letter Review:

Your engagement letter should specifically address:

  • Scope of interim and year-end procedures
  • Responsibility for internal control testing
  • Timeline for management representation letters
  • Access requirements for job sites and project documentation
  • Additional services (tax preparation, consulting, etc.)

Audit Planning Meeting Agenda:

Schedule a comprehensive planning meeting 60 days before year-end:

  • New markets entered
  • Major contract awards/completions
  • Organizational changes
  • Technology implementations

  • New accounting standards adopted

  • System upgrades or conversions

Week 2: Insurance Audits and Workers' Compensation Management

Learning Objectives:

  • Master the workers' compensation audit process and premium calculations
  • Understand general liability and other insurance audits
  • Learn advanced strategies for managing insurance costs and compliance
  • Develop expertise in certificate of insurance management and tracking

Comprehensive Lesson Content:

Insurance audits in construction can result in significant premium adjustments - often hundreds of thousands of dollars. As CFO, your understanding of the audit process and proactive management can save substantial costs while ensuring proper coverage.

Workers' Compensation Audit Deep Dive:

Understanding Premium Calculations:

Workers' compensation premiums are calculated using this formula: Premium = (Payroll ÷ $100) × Classification Rate × Experience Modification Factor × Schedule Credits/Debits

Detailed Example:

Sunrise Construction has the following annual payroll:

  • Carpenters (Class 5403): $1,200,000 at $8.50 per $100
  • Concrete Workers (Class 5213): $800,000 at $12.75 per $100
  • Office Staff (Class 8810): $300,000 at $0.35 per $100
  • Officers (Class 5606): $400,000 at $3.25 per $100

Base Premium Calculation:

  • Carpenters: ($1,200,000 ÷ 100) × $8.50 = $102,000
  • Concrete: ($800,000 ÷ 100) × $12.75 = $102,000
  • Office: ($300,000 ÷ 100) × $0.35 = $1,050
  • Officers: ($400,000 ÷ 100) × $3.25 = $13,000

Base Premium Total: $218,050

Experience Modification Factor:

If the company's experience mod is 0.92 (8% better than average): Modified Premium: $218,050 × 0.92 = $200,606

Advanced Audit Defense Strategies:

Executive Officer Exemptions:

Many states allow officers to exclude themselves from coverage:

  • Must be true officers (not just titled employees)
  • Must own minimum percentage of company
  • Must file proper exclusion forms
  • Can significantly reduce premiums for owner-operated companies

  • With exclusion: $0 premium
  • Annual Savings: $9,000

  1. Multiple Choice: Under ASC 606, which documentation is MOST critical for auditors reviewing construction revenue recognition?

a) Customer contracts and change orders b) Cash receipt records
c) Percentage completion calculations with supporting cost data d) Progress billing schedules

Answer: c) Percentage completion calculations with supporting cost data

Explanation: While all documentation is important, auditors focus most heavily on the percentage completion calculations because these directly drive revenue recognition. The supporting cost data (actual costs incurred, estimated costs to complete, and total estimated costs) must be detailed and well-supported to validate the revenue recognition calculations under ASC 606.

  1. Multiple Choice: Workers' compensation experience modification factors are calculated using:

a) Current year claims data only b) A 3-year rolling average excluding the most recent year
c) A 5-year average including all years d) Only years with claims activity

Answer: b) A 3-year rolling average excluding the most recent year

Explanation: Experience mods are calculated using a 3-year window that excludes the most recent year to allow for claims to develop. For example, the 2025 mod would use experience from 2021, 2022, and 2023, excluding 2024 to allow sufficient time for claims reporting and settlement.

  1. Short Answer: Explain the three-way match process in construction and why it's critical for fraud prevention.

Answer: The three-way match process compares three documents before authorizing payment: (1) Purchase Order showing what was ordered, (2) Receiving Report confirming what was actually received, and (3) Vendor Invoice requesting payment. This control prevents fraud by ensuring payments are only made for goods/services that were legitimately ordered, actually received, and properly invoiced. Without this control, fictitious invoices could be processed, payments could be made for undelivered goods, or pricing could be manipulated.

  1. (10 points) Explain the key differences between a financial statement audit, review, and compilation for construction companies. Include the level of assurance provided and typical cost differences.

Answer:

Financial Statement Audit: Provides highest level of assurance through extensive testing of transactions, balances, and internal controls. Auditor expresses an opinion on whether statements are fairly presented in accordance with GAAP. Includes detailed testing of WIP schedules, revenue recognition, and job costs. Week 1: Financial Audit Preparation and CPA Engagement

Learning Objectives:

  • Master comprehensive year-end audit preparation procedures for construction companies
  • Understand auditor requirements, testing methodologies, and industry-specific risks
  • Learn to prepare detailed audit work papers and supporting schedules
  • Develop expertise in managing the audit process from planning through completion

Comprehensive Lesson Content:

Financial audits in construction are significantly more complex than in other industries due to the project-based nature of operations, percentage-of-completion accounting, and unique risk factors. As CFO, your preparation and management of the audit process directly impacts the cost, duration, and outcome of the engagement.

Understanding Construction Audit Complexity:

Construction companies face unique audit challenges that require specialized preparation:

  1. Revenue Recognition Complexity: ASC 606 percentage-of-completion calculations require extensive documentation and testing
  2. Work-in-Progress Validation: Auditors must verify the accuracy of WIP schedules and underlying cost accumulation
  3. Contract Compliance: Performance obligations, change orders, and claims require detailed review
  4. Multi-Location Operations: Job sites across different states create logistical and documentation challenges
  5. Related Party Transactions: Joint ventures and partnership arrangements need careful examination

Pre-Audit Strategic Planning (90 Days Out):

Audit Firm Selection Criteria:

When selecting or evaluating your audit firm, consider these construction-specific factors:

  • Industry Experience: Minimum 25% of firm's revenue from construction clients
  • Technical Expertise: Demonstrated knowledge of ASC 606, job costing, and WIP accounting
  • Geographic Coverage: Ability to visit multiple job sites efficiently
  • Timing Flexibility: Understanding of construction's seasonal nature and project deadlines
  • Technology Integration: Compatibility with Ledgerline Intacct, JCS Construction, and other systems

Engagement Letter Review:

Your engagement letter should specifically address:

  • Scope of interim and year-end procedures
  • Responsibility for internal control testing
  • Timeline for management representation letters
  • Access requirements for job sites and project documentation
  • Additional services (tax preparation, consulting, etc.)

Audit Planning Meeting Agenda:

Schedule a comprehensive planning meeting 60 days before year-end:

Business Update (30 minutes):

  • New markets entered
  • Major contract awards/completions
  • Organizational changes
  • Technology implementations

Accounting Changes (20 minutes):

  • New accounting standards adopted
  • Changes in estimates or policies
  • System upgrades or conversions

Risk Assessment (45 minutes):

  • Project losses or disputes
  • Customer concentration changes
  • Regulatory compliance issues
  • Internal control deficiencies

Logistics Planning (15 minutes):

  • Document preparation timeline
  • Personnel availability
  • Office space and equipment needs

Supporting Schedules:

Internal Control Documentation:

Narrative Descriptions:

Revenue Recognition Process: "Monthly, project managers submit progress reports including percentage completion estimates based on costs incurred and remaining work to be performed. Week 2: Insurance Audits and Workers' Compensation Management

Learning Objectives:

  • Master the workers' compensation audit process and premium calculations
  • Understand general liability and other insurance audits
  • Learn advanced strategies for managing insurance costs and compliance
  • Develop expertise in certificate of insurance management and tracking

Comprehensive Lesson Content:

Insurance audits in construction can result in significant premium adjustments - often hundreds of thousands of dollars. As CFO, your understanding of the audit process and proactive management can save substantial costs while ensuring proper coverage.

Workers' Compensation Audit Deep Dive:

Understanding Premium Calculations:

Workers' compensation premiums are calculated using this formula: Premium = (Payroll ÷ $100) × Classification Rate × Experience Modification Factor × Schedule Credits/Debits

Detailed Example:

Sunrise Construction has the following annual payroll:

  • Carpenters (Class 5403): $1,200,000 at $8.50 per $100
  • Concrete Workers (Class 5213): $800,000 at $12.75 per $100
  • Office Staff (Class 8810): $300,000 at $0.35 per $100
  • Officers (Class 5606): $400,000 at $3.25 per $100

Base Premium Calculation:

  • Carpenters: ($1,200,000 ÷ 100) × $8.50 = $102,000
  • Concrete: ($800,000 ÷ 100) × $12.75 = $102,000
  • Office: ($300,000 ÷ 100) × $0.35 = $1,050
  • Officers: ($400,000 ÷ 100) × $3.25 = $13,000

Base Premium Total: $218,050

Experience Modification Factor:

If the company's experience mod is 0.92 (8% better than average): Modified Premium: $218,050 × 0.92 = $200,606

Advanced Audit Defense Strategies:

Executive Officer Exemptions:

Many states allow officers to exclude themselves from coverage:

  • Must be true officers (not just titled employees)
  • Must own minimum percentage of company
  • Must file proper exclusion forms
  • Can significantly reduce premiums for owner-operated companies

Example Impact: Owner draws $200,000 salary at 5606 rate of $4.50 per $100:

  • With coverage: $200,000 ÷ 100 × $4.50 = $9,000
  • With exclusion: $0 premium
  • Annual Savings: $9,000

  • Tool theft

  • Inventory shrinkage

  • Percentage completion overstatement
  • Related party transactions

Month 9 Quiz (Enhanced)

Instructions: Choose the best answer for multiple choice questions. Provide complete explanations for short-answer questions. Show all calculations for numerical problems.

  1. Multiple Choice: Under ASC 606, which documentation is MOST critical for auditors reviewing construction revenue recognition?

a) Customer contracts and change orders b) Cash receipt records
c) Percentage completion calculations with supporting cost data d) Progress billing schedules

Answer: c) Percentage completion calculations with supporting cost data

Explanation: While all documentation is important, auditors focus most heavily on the percentage completion calculations because these directly drive revenue recognition. The supporting cost data (actual costs incurred, estimated costs to complete, and total estimated costs) must be detailed and well-supported to validate the revenue recognition calculations under ASC 606.

  1. Multiple Choice: Workers' compensation experience modification factors are calculated using:

a) Current year claims data only b) A 3-year rolling average excluding the most recent year
c) A 5-year average including all years d) Only years with claims activity

Answer: b) A 3-year rolling average excluding the most recent year

Explanation: Experience mods are calculated using a 3-year window that excludes the most recent year to allow for claims to develop. For example, the 2025 mod would use experience from 2021, 2022, and 2023, excluding 2024 to allow sufficient time for claims reporting and settlement.

  1. Short Answer: Explain the three-way match process in construction and why it's critical for fraud prevention.

Answer: The three-way match process compares three documents before authorizing payment: (1) Purchase Order showing what was ordered, (2) Receiving Report confirming what was actually received, and (3) Vendor Invoice requesting payment. This control prevents fraud by ensuring payments are only made for goods/services that were legitimately ordered, actually received, and properly invoiced. Without this control, fictitious invoices could be processed, payments could be made for undelivered goods, or pricing could be manipulated.

  1. Calculation Problem: Calculate the workers' compensation premium for the following annual payroll:

Carpenters: $800,000 at Class 5403, rate $9.25 per $100 Office Staff: $200,000 at Class 8810, rate $0.45 per $100 Experience modification factor: 0.88

Show all work.

Answer:

  • Carpenters: ($800,000 ÷ 100) × $9.25 = $74,000
  • Office Staff: ($200,000 ÷ 100) × $0.45 = $900
  • Base Premium: $74,000 + $900 = $74,900
  • Modified Premium: $74,900 × 0.88 = $65,912
  1. Multiple Choice: Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply to:

a) All construction projects over $10,000 b) Federal construction projects over $2,000 c) State projects over $25,000 d) Commercial projects over $100,000

Answer: b) Federal construction projects over $2,000

Explanation: The Davis-Bacon Act specifically applies to federal construction, alteration, and repair contracts exceeding $2,000. State and local prevailing wage laws are separate requirements with different thresholds.

  1. True/False: Certified payroll reports under Davis-Bacon must be submitted monthly.

Answer: False

Explanation: Certified payroll reports (Form WH-347) must be submitted weekly, not monthly. Each report covers one work week and must be submitted to the contracting agency by the end of the week following the work week covered.

  1. Short Answer: List and explain four red flags that might indicate a ghost employee on the payroll.

Answer:

  1. No tax withholdings: Ghost employees often use fake SSNs that don't generate tax withholdings
  2. Same address as supervisor: May indicate supervisor is creating fictitious employees
  3. Perfect attendance: Never calls in sick, takes vacation, or has any absences (unrealistic)
  4. Round number hours: Always works exactly 40 hours, 80 hours, etc. (lacks natural variation)

Month 9 Test (Enhanced)

Part A: Multiple Choice (20 points - 2 points each)

  1. When preparing for a construction company audit, which schedule requires the MOST detailed supporting documentation?

a) Accounts receivable aging b) Work-in-progress analysis c) Fixed asset rollforward d) Accounts payable listing

Answer: b) Work-in-progress analysis

Explanation: The WIP analysis is the most complex and critical schedule for construction audits, requiring detailed support for costs incurred, estimated costs to complete, percentage completion calculations, and revenue recognition. Auditors spend significant time testing these calculations as they directly impact financial statement accuracy.

  1. Which factor has the GREATEST impact on workers' compensation premium calculations?

a) Number of employees b) Employee classification codes c) Experience modification factor
d) Geographic location

Answer: b) Employee classification codes

Explanation: Classification codes determine the base rates, which can vary dramatically (from $0.35 per $100 for office workers to $25+ per $100 for roofers). While experience mods can adjust premiums by ±50%, classification codes create the foundational rate differential that often exceeds 5,000% between the lowest and highest risk classes.

  1. In a three-way match system, which document should be created FIRST?

a) Purchase order b) Receiving report
c) Vendor invoice d) Payment authorization

Answer: a) Purchase order

Explanation: The purchase order must be created first as it represents the authorized commitment to purchase goods/services. It serves as the control document against which receiving reports and vendor invoices are matched to ensure only authorized purchases are paid.

  1. Under the Davis-Bacon Act, fringe benefits can be satisfied by:

a) Cash payments only b) Bona fide benefit plans only c) Either cash payments or bona fide benefit plans d) Neither - fringe requirements cannot be satisfied

Answer: c) Either cash payments or bona fide benefit plans

Explanation: Davis-Bacon allows contractors flexibility in meeting fringe benefit requirements. They can provide actual benefits (health insurance, pension, etc.) equal to the prevailing rate, pay additional cash wages, or use a combination of both methods.

  1. Which internal control weakness would be classified as a Material Weakness?

a) Missing signatures on purchase orders under $1,000 b) Untimely monthly account reconciliations c) Lack of segregation of duties in cash receipts and disbursements d) Inadequate documentation of policy updates

Answer: c) Lack of segregation of duties in cash receipts and disbursements

Explanation: Material weaknesses create a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement in the financial statements could occur and not be prevented or detected timely. Lack of segregation in cash handling creates significant fraud risk and potential for material errors.

Part B: Short Answer Problems (30 points)

  1. (10 points) Explain the key differences between a financial statement audit, review, and compilation for construction companies. Include the level of assurance provided and typical cost differences.

Answer:

Financial Statement Audit: Provides highest level of assurance through extensive testing of transactions, balances, and internal controls. Auditor expresses an opinion on whether statements are fairly presented in accordance with GAAP. Includes detailed testing of WIP schedules, revenue recognition, and job costs. Typically costs $50,000-$200,000+ depending on company size and complexity.

Review: Provides limited assurance based on analytical procedures and inquiries. No opinion is expressed, only negative assurance ("nothing came to our attention"). Less testing of detailed transactions and internal controls. Typically costs 30-50% less than an audit.
